subject: math
description: Students construct an equilateral triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon inscribed in a given circle using only a compass and straightedge, and reason about the resulting figures. They justify each construction step (why a chord equal to the radius cuts a $60^\circ$ arc, why perpendicular diameters give a square), order the steps correctly, and compute the exact side lengths, central angles, perimeters, and areas of the inscribed polygons in terms of the circle's radius $r$.
subSkills: Recall that a chord equal in length to the radius subtends a $60^\circ$ central angle, so stepping the radius around a circle of radius $r$ yields six points (the regular hexagon)
Construct a regular hexagon by marking off arcs of radius $r$ around the circle, then connect every vertex
Construct an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle by connecting every other hexagon vertex (joining alternate $60^\circ$ points to span $120^\circ$ arcs)
Construct a square inscribed in a circle by drawing two perpendicular diameters (a diameter and its perpendicular bisector) and connecting the four endpoints
Justify each step from the postulates: all radii equal, the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the center, inscribed/central angle relationships
Compute the central angle of a regular $n$-gon as $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$ and the inscribed (vertex) angle as $\frac{(n-2)180^\circ}{n}$
Derive exact side length, perimeter, and area of the inscribed polygon in terms of radius $r$ using $30$-$60$-$90$ and $45$-$45$-$90$ triangles

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the next construction step
problemArchetypes.example: You are inscribing a regular hexagon in a circle of radius $r$. After drawing the circle and marking a point $A$ on it, what is the correct next step? (Set the compass to the radius $r$ and strike an arc from $A$ to locate the next vertex.)

problemArchetypes.name: Justify why a step works
problemArchetypes.example: When inscribing a hexagon, why does setting the compass width equal to the radius locate a vertex exactly $60^\circ$ away? (The radius, the new radius, and the chord form an equilateral triangle, so the central angle is $60^\circ$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Central / interior angle of the inscribed polygon
problemArchetypes.example: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle. What central angle does each side subtend at the center? ($\frac{360^\circ}{3}=120^\circ$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Side length in terms of radius
problemArchetypes.example: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. Find the exact side length of the square. (Side $=r\sqrt{2}$, from the $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle formed by two radii.)

problemArchetypes.name: Perimeter or area in terms of radius
problemArchetypes.example: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. Find its perimeter and area. (Perimeter $=6r$; area $=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}r^2$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Order the full construction
problemArchetypes.example: Place the steps for inscribing a square in a circle in correct order: draw a diameter, construct its perpendicular bisector through the center, mark the four intersections with the circle, connect consecutive intersection points.

Easy.description: Single-fact recall and one-step recognition tied to the three named constructions. Student names a tool action, reads off a central angle from $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$, or recalls the radius-equals-side fact for the hexagon. No multi-step computation.
constraints: Identify which polygon ($n=3,4,6$) a described construction produces, or the single next step
Compute a central angle $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$ for $n\in\{3,4,6\}$ as an integer number of degrees
Recall that the hexagon side equals the radius $r$ and its perimeter is $6r$
Tools limited to compass and straightedge; one idea per item

Medium.description: Two-step reasoning: derive a side length or interior angle, or justify a single construction step using equilateral-triangle or perpendicular-bisector reasoning. Requires a $30$-$60$-$90$ or $45$-$45$-$90$ relationship.
constraints: Find an exact side length such as $r\sqrt{2}$ (square) or $r\sqrt{3}$ (equilateral triangle) from a right triangle inside the circle
Give a one-sentence justification for why the radius-step yields $60^\circ$ or why perpendicular diameters yield a square
Answers are exact radicals in terms of $r$, never rounded decimals

Hard.description: Multi-step synthesis: compute area in terms of $r$, order an entire construction, or chain a justification with a numeric result. Student combines the angle facts with right-triangle trig or apothem reasoning and may compare two of the three inscribed polygons.
constraints: Derive exact area, e.g. hexagon $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}r^2$, square $2r^2$, equilateral triangle $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2$
Order a complete 4-to-6 step compass-and-straightedge construction
Use the apothem $a=r\cos\!\frac{180^\circ}{n}$ or split into congruent isosceles triangles
May require comparing perimeters or areas of two inscribed polygons in the same circle

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: Single ramped worksheet. If split: tier1 covers Easy to Medium (naming constructions, next-step recognition, central/interior angles, hexagon side $=r$, square side $r\sqrt{2}$); tier2 covers Medium to Hard (exact side/perimeter/area derivations, full step ordering, justifications, two-polygon comparisons).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks stepping the radius around the circle gives the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle rather than a hexagon
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the radius-length chord cuts a $120^\circ$ arc and yields a triangle, so a chord of length $r$ is the triangle's side instead of the hexagon's side

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the central angle $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$ with the interior (vertex) angle $\frac{(n-2)180^\circ}{n}$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For the inscribed square reports the central angle as $90^\circ$ but the interior angle also as $90^\circ$ where the central is asked, e.g. gives $60^\circ$ for the hexagon's central angle by using $\frac{(6-2)180^\circ}{6}=120^\circ$ in the wrong slot

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the diameter $2r$ as the inscribed square's side instead of computing the chord
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the square side as $2r$ (the diameter) instead of $r\sqrt{2}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student forgets to take the reciprocal of the radius relationship and uses $\sin/\cos$ on the wrong angle, getting $r\sqrt{3}$ for the square
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes the square side as $r\sqrt{3}$ (the equilateral triangle's side) by using a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle where a $45$-$45$-$90$ applies

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the inscribed equilateral triangle's side as equal to the radius (like the hexagon)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States the equilateral triangle side is $r$ instead of $r\sqrt{3}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student computes a regular polygon area with the circle formula $\pi r^2$ instead of the polygon's exact radical area
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives the inscribed hexagon area as $\pi r^2$ or $6r^2$ instead of $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}r^2$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student orders the square construction wrong, connecting diameter endpoints before constructing the perpendicular bisector
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a step order that joins the two endpoints of a single diameter (giving a line, not four vertices) before any perpendicular is drawn
